Food insecurity (%)

How to read this chart. The line is a linear trend and r is the Pearson correlation between the two county estimates. These are county-level (ecological) associations: they show where conditions cluster, not that food insecurity causes these conditions in individuals. The correlations are also high partly by design: PLACES models every measure from the same population characteristics (age, sex, race and ethnicity) and county poverty, so its county estimates tend to move together.

About

Row

About this dashboard

Question

Where in Georgia are cardiometabolic conditions and food insecurity most common, and do they appear in the same counties?

Data

CDC PLACES: County Data (GIS Friendly Format), 2025 release (data.cdc.gov, dataset i46a-9kgh). PLACES provides model-based estimates for every US county, built from 2023 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) data and census population data. The six measures refer to adults aged 18 and older: obesity, diagnosed diabetes, high blood pressure, coronary heart disease, no leisure-time physical activity and food insecurity in the past 12 months.

Methods

  • I used age-adjusted prevalence, so counties with older or younger populations can be compared fairly.
  • Maps and rankings show each county’s estimate with its 95% confidence interval.
  • The Georgia value is the average of the 159 county estimates weighted by each county’s adult population. It is a reference point, not an official state estimate.
  • The scatter plots show Pearson correlations between county estimates.

Limitations

PLACES estimates are modeled, not direct survey counts, so small counties have wider confidence intervals. Because every measure is modeled from the same population characteristics and county poverty, estimates for different measures are strongly correlated partly by design. County-level correlations do not show individual-level relationships or causation.

Tools

R (dplyr, tidyr, readr, jsonlite, htmltools, glue), flexdashboard and JavaScript. County boundaries come from the GeoJSON file published by plotly. The code is on GitHub.

Author

Maria Alvarez-Nuncio, MPH (Global Health, Emory University). LinkedIn · Portfolio
